[MUJAHID:v1p262#3/r1] MUJAHID, d. 104 · مجاهد | reports | Mujahid identifies those who return to disbelief as Quraysh at Badr and earlier peoples who had met the established fate.
[MUQATIL:8:38-40/r1] MUQATIL, d. 150 · author | holds | If unbelievers stop associating partners with God and repent, their pre-Islamic acts of associating partners are forgiven.
[MUQATIL:8:38-40/r2] MUQATIL, d. 150 · author | holds | If they return to fighting the Prophet without repenting, the precedent of earlier peoples is their killing at Badr; the warning is meant to prevent another such return.
[SIBAWAYH:وإنلمتجعلهبمنزلةاسمليسفيهالهاءلميتغيرعنحالهالتيكان#331/r1] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | When a name ending in tāʾ marbūṭa is treated after truncation as a name without it, عرقوة and قمحدوة yield عرقى and قمحدى.
[SIBAWAYH:وإنلمتجعلهبمنزلةاسمليسفيهالهاءلميتغيرعنحالهالتيكان#331/r10] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | Names such as حارث, مالك, and عامر are especially often shortened because they are frequent personal names and common in poetry; several poets attest them.
[SIBAWAYH:وإنلمتجعلهبمنزلةاسمليسفيهالهاءلميتغيرعنحالهالتيكان#331/r11] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | Any proper name may be shortened in address; examples include يزيد as يزى, ليلى as ليل, and لميس as لمى.
[SIBAWAYH:وإنلمتجعلهبمنزلةاسمليسفيهالهاءلميتغيرعنحالهالتيكان#331/r12] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | Imruʾ al-Qays's verse uses طريف بن مال for طريف بن مالك, showing a name without tāʾ may also be shortened in poetry.
[SIBAWAYH:وإنلمتجعلهبمنزلةاسمليسفيهالهاءلميتغيرعنحالهالتيكان#331/r13] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | reports | The text cites a line attributed to Ṭarafa as a constructed example by an ʿĀbidī poet, with سعد shortened from أسعد.
[SIBAWAYH:وإنلمتجعلهبمنزلةاسمليسفيهالهاءلميتغيرعنحالهالتيكان#331/r14] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | reports | Sībawayh reports al-Khalīl's rule that names are shortened from five letters to four and four to three, with three-letter names as the lower limit.
[SIBAWAYH:وإنلمتجعلهبمنزلةاسمليسفيهالهاءلميتغيرعنحالهالتيكان#331/r15] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | Only dominant proper names without tāʾ are normally shortened, since they are frequent enough to undergo deletion even outside address, as in زيد بن عمرو.
[SIBAWAYH:وإنلمتجعلهبمنزلةاسمليسفيهالهاءلميتغيرعنحالهالتيكان#331/r16] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | يا صاح for صاحب is an exceptional shortening justified by frequent use, like the conventional reductions لم أبل, لم يك, and لا أدر.
[SIBAWAYH:وإنلمتجعلهبمنزلةاسمليسفيهالهاءلميتغيرعنحالهالتيكان#331/r2] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | The same truncation analysis gives يا رعى from رعوم and يا قطا from قطوان.
[SIBAWAYH:وإنلمتجعلهبمنزلةاسمليسفيهالهاءلميتغيرعنحالهالتيكان#331/r3] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | طفاوة becomes يا طفاء when the remainder is treated as a name without tāʾ, because the language has no noun with that final pattern.
[SIBAWAYH:وإنلمتجعلهبمنزلةاسمليسفيهالهاءلميتغيرعنحالهالتيكان#331/r4] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | If the remaining wāw is not made an inflectional ending, it stays unchanged after truncating طفاوة: يا طفاو.
[SIBAWAYH:وإنلمتجعلهبمنزلةاسمليسفيهالهاءلميتغيرعنحالهالتيكان#331/r5] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | Treating the remainder as a noun without tāʾ is less common; speakers more often preserve its form because case endings elsewhere change.
[SIBAWAYH:وإنلمتجعلهبمنزلةاسمليسفيهالهاءلميتغيرعنحالهالتيكان#331/r6] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | The truncation يا معا from معاوية is supported by al-ʿAjjāj's verse, showing that this treatment is native Arabic.
[SIBAWAYH:وإنلمتجعلهبمنزلةاسمليسفيهالهاءلميتغيرعنحالهالتيكان#331/r7] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | حيوة becomes يا حيو; in the nominative its wāw remains by the original pattern غزو, so the change is not obligatory.
[SIBAWAYH:وإنلمتجعلهبمنزلةاسمليسفيهالهاءلميتغيرعنحالهالتيكان#331/r8] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | One may not drop tāʾ and treat the remainder as masculine for an ordinary feminine noun, since that would confuse gender; the exception is a dominant proper name.
[SIBAWAYH:وإنلمتجعلهبمنزلةاسمليسفيهالهاءلميتغيرعنحالهالتيكان#331/r9] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | Truncation of names not ending in tāʾ is less common because it removes both tanwin and an inherent final consonant, though it is permitted.

item.text: The notes cover several separate issues: who is addressed, what ending and returning mean, the promised pardon, and the threatened precedent. They also include grammar, readings, and legal applications. I’m keeping those questions distinct while collecting notes that give the same answer.
